@@131410230 <h> Share : <p> When I was a journalism student -- both in my undergraduate and postgraduate days -- the BBC was more than a broadcaster . It was our language teacher and a reference point for what was called global standards in reporting . That did n't mean the BBC was unbiased ; it meant it appeared to construct balance through careful sourcing , tone , and structure . In our classrooms , the BBC stood as an example of how professionalism could lend credibility to news . " Watch the BBC , " teachers often said , " that 's where you learn balance . " <p> But today , the same institution once admired for its balance is at the centre of an unending storm . Across mainstream and alternative media , the narrative around the BBC is saturated with charges of bias -- overt or covert , left or right , moral or political . Every new controversy , from the Trump speech edit to the Israel -- Gaza coverage , is treated as evidence that the BBC has " lost its neutrality . " Yet @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ This moment is not only about whether the BBC is biased or not ; it is about how the very idea of ethical journalism should be understood in a world where bias is not a failure , but a condition of storytelling itself . <p> Beyond the " Bias " Frame <p> Most online discussions focus narrowly on whether the BBC crossed the line of impartiality -- whether it misrepresented Donald Trump 's speech , or leaned against Israel in its Gaza coverage . These might be serious lapses , but reducing them to " proof of bias " simplifies the problem . <p> The BBC episode should serve as a reminder -- and a provocation -- for journalists and media students alike . It invites us to rethink how ethical awareness actually operates inside newsrooms . Bias , after all , is rarely born of bad faith ; it often emerges from perception -- shaped by culture , values , and editorial judgment . Every choice , from headline to source selection , carries a worldview . The goal of journalism , then , can not be to erase @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ recognise its presence , question its influence , and keep it accountable . Ethics in journalism is not about claiming neutrality , but about negotiating honesty within one 's perspective . <p> The Language of Neutrality <p> This brings us to the BBC 's latest controversy -- and to the politics of language itself . Critics often point out that the BBC avoided calling Hamas " terrorists , " while it freely used the term for the 9/11 attackers . For many , that contrast exposes hypocrisy . Yet the more pressing issue is n't whether the BBC took the " right " side , but how language shapes what we consider legitimate , violent , or newsworthy . Words like terrorist , militant , or freedom fighter do more than describe events -- they signal moral and political positions . In that sense , the BBC 's word choices reveal not just bias , but the impossible tension between neutrality and meaning . <p> From Neutrality to Awareness <p> The BBC , like any media organization , has every right to take a stand -- to challenge Donald Trump @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . Journalism is not meant to be emotionless or blind to power . But what makes such positions credible is not their political direction , but their ethical depth -- the awareness of how stories are sourced , verified , and framed . When that awareness slips , bias turns into distortion . The goal , therefore , is n't to run from bias , but to confront it responsibly . Ethical journalism is not about escaping bias , but about consciously engaging with it -- questioning where it comes from , how it operates , and what consequences it carries , every single day . <p> When Gatekeeping Fails <p> The Trump speech edit might look like a small mistake -- a few missing words that went unnoticed in the rush of production . Yet those omissions changed the moral tone of the story entirely . Whether this was a simple oversight or a lapse in editorial gatekeeping is open to debate . But it does raise an important question : how do such slips pass through multiple layers of review in one of the world 's most respected @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ speed with scrutiny . When those filters weaken -- through haste , assumption , or overconfidence -- credibility begins to fray . This is why gatekeeping today needs to be revisited , not as a mechanism of control , but as a safeguard of trust . Because in journalism , trust is never automatic ; it 's earned in every edit , every frame , and every word . <p> Rethinking the Lesson <p> If you ask an AI system whether the BBC is biased , it will probably say yes -- because that 's what most of the online news data suggests . But journalism should n't be about echoing data ; it should be about asking better questions . Instead of joining the noise of " BBC is biased " or " BBC is neutral , " media students and professionals need to dig deeper : biased in what way , through which choices , and under what pressures ? <p> The BBC case is n't a verdict -- it 's a classroom . It reminds us that ethical journalism is not about chasing purity but about practicing @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ every frame carries its own weight of meaning . So rather than outsourcing judgment to algorithms or outrage , each of us has to study , interpret , and reach our own conclusions . That 's not only good media literacy -- that 's the beginning of being a responsible journalist .

@@131469815 <h> Share : <p> Author 's NoteI wrote this essay to show what really happened when Richard Falk and Hilal Elver were detained at the Canadian border ? -- ? and to explore what it reveals about power , accountability , and the fight to speak truth to authority . <p> Introduction : Two Scholars Detained , A Truth Confronted <p> Richard Falk has spent the better part of a century inside the world 's most serious rooms : the United Nations , the International Court of Justice , the international legal tribunals where the language of war , occupation , and human rights is hammered into shape . <p> At ninety-five , he carries his papers in neat folders and moves with the slow care of a man who has spent a lifetime thinking rather than rushing . " <p> Even as the Tribunal they were heading to in Ottawa gathered evidence and testimony , the state sought to preempt its impact at the very border . What followed was an interrogation of Falk and Elver that revealed a troubling conflation of Canada 's national security with ideological alignment to Israel . <p> The questions came one after another , circling obsessively around the same forbidden center : * " What exactly will you be saying about Israel in Ottawa ? " * " Why did your UN reports criticize Israeli military actions ? " * " Have you been in contact with Palestinian organizations ? " * " What is your position on the war in Gaza ? " * " Who invited you to this Tribunal , and why ? " <p> The line of questioning was so singularly focused on defending Israeli policy that it betrayed a fundamental confusion @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ? -- ? not a single question about contraband , immigration status , visas , residency , or criminal history.Everything was about Israel . <p> Halfway through the four-hour ordeal , the absurdity sharpened into recognition : nothing Falk or Elver had ever written posed any threat to Canada . But everything they had documented about Israeli conduct ? -- ? settlement expansion , blockade , collective punishment , starvation ? -- ? posed a threat to Israel 's political security , and therefore , in the logic that now governs Canadian institutions , to Canada itself . <p> In that moment , the interrogation ceased to be absurd.It became coherent ? -- ? chillingly so . <p> Canada had collapsed the boundary between its own national security and Israel 's political narrative ? -- ? the border itself enforcing it . <p> This transformation did not happen overnight . It is the product of a political logic constructed over decades . -- <p> How Political Loyalty In Canada Becomes a Matter of National Security <p> First , criticism of Israel has been steadily recast as a security issue , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , B'nai Brith , and the Friends of Simon Wiesenthal Center ? -- ? which explicitly identify as Jewish and advocate for the preservation of Israel as an apartheid Jewish state ? -- ? have spent years briefing Canadian politicians , police , and security agencies with the claim that Palestinian solidarity , criticism of Israeli occupation , or support for boycotts constitutes " extremism " or " potential radicalization . " <p> These same zionist organizations have shaped Canadian security discourse in ways that conflate Palestinian advocacy with extremism . <p> Second , Canadian governments have elevated support for Israel from a diplomatic position to a pillar of national identity . Israel is framed as a frontline state in the " war on terror , " a democratic ally in a dangerous world . Once foreign policy is securitized ( treated as a national security matter ) , ordinary political disagreements ? -- ? like criticizing Israeli policies ? -- ? are portrayed as destabilizing or threatening to Canada itself , even when they clearly pose no real risk . <p> Third , Canadian institutions increasingly outsource their concept @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ monitor their cues , amplify their alarms , and follow their frame . <p> This posture is rooted in a complex blend of geopolitical alignment , domestic political calculations , and a shared settler-colonial history that makes Canada 's political establishment uniquely sensitive to challenges of Israel 's legitimacy . <p> We have seen this pattern before . The same choreography that silenced a local activist in Vancouver was now being deployed at the national border against a former UN official . The system , it seems , operates the same way whether the target is a grassroots organizer or an international jurist. -- <p> Charlotte Kates : A Domestic Parallel When Vancouver activist Charlotte Kates praised Palestinian resistance at a rally in 2024 , nothing happened immediately . Police did not arrest her , prosecutors did not open a file . <p> But within hours , B'nai Brith had clipped her speech , declared it a threat , and demanded action . CIJA echoed the alarm . Held at the University of Ottawa 's Human Rights Research and Education Centre , it brought together over fifty witnesses : survivors from Gaza , Palestinian @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Canadian lawyers working on arms exports and sanctions obligations . <p> The Tribunal stands squarely in the lineage of historic people 's tribunals , translating past lessons into direct scrutiny of Canada 's policies . Experts traced Canadian-made components in Israeli drones and jets . Lawyers detailed Canada 's obligations under the Genocide Convention and its failures to meet them . Most of it comes from the value of Tesla and SpaceX shares . These are digital entries that reflect what people think the companies are worth . <p> They can not simply be turned into endless supplies of food , water or housing the moment someone demands it.To make this clearer , the post used a simple example . If Musk suddenly tried to buy " 700 billion pounds of food " @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . Instead , food prices would surge because everyone would now be competing with a massive new buyer . That would mean fewer groceries for ordinary families and shortages in places that were managing fine before.The post also explained that real resources are limited . You can not conjure more farmers , trucks , wheat fields or factories just by spending money . If you need millions of tonnes of extra food or a huge new water system , the workers , land and materials must be taken from some other activity , such as manufacturing , construction or services.This is where the idea of opportunity cost comes in . When billions are poured into one sector , those people and resources must leave other jobs to meet the new demand . In other words , creating more of one thing always means creating less of something else . Large-scale aid is not simply a matter of writing a cheque . It involves reshaping entire industries , supply chains and labour markets , often with unpredictable side effects.The post argued that these basic economic realities are often overlooked in celebrity @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ because a billionaire exists . <h> The backlash against celebrity economics <p> Others pointed out the inconsistencies in Eilish 's argument . Critics asked why the singer , with an estimated net worth of around $50 million , had not herself addressed smaller-scale crises . Some noted that if the logic applies to Musk , it applies on a proportional level to every wealthy entertainer.Free-market commentators also argued that turning billionaires into moral scapegoats oversimplifies structural issues such as corruption , war , supply chains and political instability . These challenges can not be solved by a single large cheque , regardless of who writes it.Huge financial interventions often cause distortions . Flooding a region with aid can displace local markets , raise prices or undermine farmers , builders or manufacturers who are already operating there.Solving world hunger or rebuilding Gaza requires logistics , political solutions and thousands of coordinated workers , not merely a wealthy individual deciding to pay for it . <h> A broader debate about wealth , morality and responsibility <p> The Eilish and Musk controversy ultimately highlights a deep public confusion about how modern wealth works @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of cash waiting to be spent . Most of it can not be liquidated without damaging the companies that create that wealth in the first place.Critics of Musk are quick to argue that this does not remove moral responsibility . Wealthy individuals can , and often do , fund high-impact charities , invest in renewable technologies or support innovation . Yet even billionaire philanthropy has limits and trade-offs that celebrity campaigns often overlook . <h> The conversation is not going away <p> Eilish 's post struck a nerve because it tapped into a broader unease about inequality , corporate power and political gridlock . Musk 's defenders argue she oversimplified a complex issue , while her supporters say she is asking the right moral questions even if the economics are more complicated.What remains clear is that the debate over billionaire wealth , what it is , what it is not and what it should be used for , is far from over .

This directly contradicts the concept of " sustainable solutions " on which the international protection system is based . <p> The UK government 's plan also undermines asylum seekers ' basic right to a decent standard of living . It proposes abolishing the legal obligation to provide housing and financial assistance , shifting these from protected entitlements to matters left to the Home Office 's discretion . This would make essential rights such as shelter and food vulnerable to political change and arbitrary administrative decisions , placing thousands of asylum seekers and their families at risk of homelessness , poverty , and destitution . <p> This deliberate regression on guarantees of adequate housing and living standards is inconsistent with the UK 's obligations under the International @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ established interpretations of the right to adequate housing . @@131662026 <h> South Africa 's G20 Presidency and the Global South Continuum <p> South Africa 's G20 Presidency represents a landmark moment for Africa and the broader Global South , building on the momentum generated by preceding Global South chairs , Indonesia , India , and Brazil . With South Africa taking charge in 2025 , the G20 will complete an uninterrupted four-year run of Global South presidencies . " <p> Gaza is a textbook case . <h> The long legal effort to suppress ecocide <p> In The Obliteration Doctrine , I show in painful detail how Lemkin had to compromise this idea . @@131823152 <h> Share : <p> At the dawning of the British Empire in 1818 , the romantic poet Percy Bysshe Shelley penned a memorable sonnet freighted with foreboding about the inevitable decline of all empires , whether in ancient Egypt or then-modern Britain . <p> In Shelly 's stanzas , a traveler in Egypt comes across the ruins of a once-monumental statue , with " a shattered visage lying half sunk " in desert sands bearing the " sneer of cold command . " Only its " trunkless legs of stone " remain standing . Yet the inscription carved on those stones still proclaims : " My name is Ozymandias , King of Kings : Look on my works , ye Mighty , and despair ! " And in a silent mockery of such imperial hubris , all the trappings of that awesome power , all the palaces and fortresses , have been utterly erased , leaving only a desolation " boundless and bare " as " the lone and level sands stretch far away . " <p> Taken too literally , those verses might lead us to anticipate some future @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the banks of the Thames River in London or stones from the Washington Monument strewn in a kudzu-covered field near the Potomac . Shelley is , however , offering us a more profound lesson that every empire teaches and every imperialist then forgets : Imperial ascent begets an inevitable decline . <p> Imperial Washington <p> Indeed , these days Donald Trump 's Washington abounds with monuments to overblown imperial grandeur and plans for more , all of which add up to an unconvincing denial that America 's global imperium is facing an Ozymandias-like fate . With his future Gilded Age ballroom meant to rise from the rubble of the White House 's East Wing , his plans for a massive triumphal arch at the city 's entrance , and a military parade of tanks and troops clanking down Constitution Avenue on his birthday , who could ever imagine such a thing ? Not Donald Trump , that 's for sure . <p> In a celebration of his " works " that are supposedly making the " mighty despair " in foreign capitals around the world , his former national security @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Foreign Affairs that the president 's " policy of peace through strength " is reversing a Democrat-induced decline of U.S. global power . According to O'Brien , instead of crippling NATO ( as his critics claim ) , President Trump is " leading the biggest European rearmament of the postwar era " ; unleashing military innovation " to counter China " ; and proving himself the " indispensable global statesman by driving efforts to bring peace to ... long-standing disputes " in Gaza , the Congo , and , quite soon , Ukraine as well . Even in North America , according to O'Brien , Trump 's attempt to acquire Greenland has forced Denmark to expand its military presence , putting Russia on notice that the West will compete for control of the Arctic . <p> As it happens , whatever the truth of any of that may be , the policy elements that O'Brien cites are certain to prove largely irrelevant to the ceaseless struggle for geopolitical power among the globe 's great empires . Or , to borrow a favorite Trumpian epithet from the president 's " cornucopia @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ world of grand strategy , none of those factors amounts to a hill of " shit . " <p> Indeed , O'Brien 's epic catalogue of Trump 's supposed foreign policy successes cleverly avoids any mention of the central factor in the rise and fall of every dominant world power for the past 500 years : energy . While the United States made genuine strides toward a green energy revolution under President Joe Biden , his successor , the " drill , baby , drill " president , has seemed determined not just to destroy those gains , but to revert to dependence on fossil fuels " bigly , " as Trump would say . In a perplexing paradox , President Trump 's systematic attack on alternative energy at home will almost certainly subvert America 's geopolitical power abroad . How and why ? Let me explain by dipping my toes in a bit of history . <p> For the past five centuries , the rise of every global empire has rested on an underlying transformation ( or perhaps revolution would be a more accurate word for it ) in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ world economy . Innovation in the basic force behind its rising global presence gave each successive hegemonic power -- Portugal , Spain , England , the United States , and possibly now China -- a critical competitive advantage , cutting costs and increasing profits . That energy innovation and the lucrative commerce it created infused each successive imperium with intangible but substantial power , impelling its armed forces relentlessly forward and crushing resistance to its rule , whether by local groups or would-be imperial rivals . Although scholars of imperial history often ignore it , energy should be considered , as I argued in my book To Govern the Globe , the determinative factor in the rise and fall of every global hegemon for the past five centuries . <p> Iberia 's Mastery of Muscle <p> In the fifteenth century , the Iberian powers -- Portugal and Spain -- manipulated the ocean winds and maximized the energy output of the human body , giving them new forms of energy that allowed their arid lands and limited populations to conquer much of the globe . By replacing the square sail of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ vessels like the famed caravela de armada doubled their capacity to tack close to the wind , allowing them to master the world 's oceans . <p> By 1500 , Portuguese warships had navigation instruments that allowed them to cross the widest bodies of water , sails to beat into the strongest headwinds , a sturdy hull for guns and cargo , and lethal cannons that could destroy enemy fleets or breach the walls of port cities . As a result , a small flotilla of Portuguese caravels soon conquered colonies on both sides of the South Atlantic Ocean and seized control of Asian sea lanes from the Red Sea to the Java Sea . <p> For the next three centuries , such sailing ships would transport 11 million African captives across the Atlantic to work as slaves in a new form of agriculture that was both exceptionally cruel and extraordinarily profitable : the sugar plantation . The output of Europe 's free yeoman farmers was then constrained by the limits of the individual body and the temperate climate 's short six-month growing season . By contrast , enslaved laborers @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ driven year-round to the brink of death and beyond to extract unprecedented productivity and profits from those plantations . Indeed , even as late as the nineteenth century , the U.S. southern slave plantation was , according to an econometric analysis , 35% more efficient than a northern family farm . <p> After developing the sugar plantation , or fazenda , as a new form of agribusiness on small islands off the coast of Africa in the fifteenth century , the Portuguese brought that system to Brazil in the sixteenth century . From there , it migrated to European colonies in the Caribbean , making that cruel commerce synonymous with the slave trade for nearly four centuries . So profitable was the slave plantation for its owners that , unlike almost every other form of production , it did not die from natural economic causes but would instead require the full force of the British navy to do it in . <p> The Dutch Harness the Winds <p> But the true masters of wind power would prove to be the Dutch , whose technological prowess would allow their small land @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ empire that spanned three continents . In the seventeenth century , the Dutch drive for scientific innovation led them to harness the winds as never before , building sailing ships 10 times the size of a Portuguese caravel and windmills that , among other things , replaced the tedious hand sawing of logs to produce lumber for shipbuilding . With giant sails spanning over 90 feet , a five-ton shaft generating up to 50 horsepower , and several sawing frames with six steel blades each , a windmill 's four-man crew could turn 60 tree trunks a day into uniform planks to maintain the massive Dutch merchant fleet of 4,000 ocean-going ships . <p> By 1650 , the Zaan district near Amsterdam , arguably Europe 's first major industrial area , had more than 50 wind-driven sawmills and was the world 's largest shipyard , launching 150 hulls annually ( at half the cost of English-built vessels ) . Many of these were the Dutch-designedfluitschip , an agile three-masted cargo vessel that cut crew size , doubled sailing speed , and could carry 500 tons of cargo with exceptional efficiency @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ power , tiny Holland defeated the mighty Spanish empire in the Thirty Years War ( 1618-48 ) , then fought the British to a standstill in three massive naval wars , while building an empire that reached around the world -- from the Spice Islands of Indonesia to the city of New Amsterdam on the island of Manhattan . <p> When Coal Was King <p> As Holland 's commercial empire began to fade , however , Great Britain was already launching an energy transition to coal-fired steam energy that would leave the wind and muscle power of the Iberian age in the dust of history . And the industrial revolution that went with it would build the world 's first truly global empire . <p> The Scottish inventor James Watt perfected the steam engine by 1784 . Such machines began driving railways in 1825 and the Royal Navy 's warships in the 1840s . By then , an armada of steam engines was transforming the nature of work worldwide -- driving sawmills , pulling gang plows , and sculpting the earth 's surface with steam shovels , steam dredges , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ number of steam engines in the United States would triple from 56,000 units to 156,000 , accounting for 77% of all American industrial power . To fuel that age of steam and steel , Britain 's coal production climbed to a peak of 290 million tons in 1913 , while worldwide production reached 1.3 billion tons . <p> Coal was the catalyst for an industrial revolution that fused steam technology with steel production to make Britain the master of the world 's oceans . From the end of the Napoleonic wars in 1815 until the outbreak of World War I in 1914 , tiny Britain with just 40 million people would preside over a global empire that controlled a quarter of all humanity directly through colonies and another quarter indirectly through client states . In addition to its vast territorial empire , Britannia ruled the world 's waves , while its pound sterling became the global reserve currency , and London the financial center of the planet . <p> America 's Petrol-Powered Hegemony <p> Just as Britain 's imperial age had coincided with its coal-driven industrial revolution , so Washington @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the voracious energy needs of its global economy . By 1950 , in the wake of World War II , the U.S. petrol-powered economy was producing half the world 's economic output and using that raw economic power for commercial and military dominion over most of the planet ( outside the Sino-Soviet communist bloc ) . <p> By 1960 , the Pentagon had built a nuclear triad that gave it a formidable strategic deterrent , as five nuclear-powered submarines armed with atomic warheads trolled the ocean depths , while 14 nuclear-armed aircraft carriers patrolled the world 's oceans . Flying from 500 U.S. overseas military bases , the Strategic Air Command had 1,700 bombers ready for nuclear strikes . <p> As American automobile ownership climbed from 40 million units in 1950 to 200 million in 2000 , the country 's oil consumption surged from 6.5 million barrels daily to a peak of 20 million . During those same decades , the federal government spent $370 billion to cover the country with 46,000 miles of interstate highways , allowing cars and trucks to replace railroads as the ribs of the nation @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of Washington 's world order , there would be a dramatic , five-fold increase in the global consumption of liquid fossil fuels during the last half of the twentieth century . As the number of motor vehicles worldwide kept climbing , crude oil rose from 27% of global fossil-fuel consumption in 1950 to 44% by 2003 , surpassing coal to become the world 's main source of energy . <p> To meet this relentlessly rising demand , the Middle East 's share of global oil production climbed from just 7% in 1945 to 35% in 2003 . As the self-appointed guardian of the Persian Gulf whose vast oil reserves represented some 60% of the world 's total , Washington would become embroiled in endless wars in that tumultuous region , from the Gulf War of 1990-91 to its present-day interventions in Israel and Iran . <p> Whether thanks to Britain 's coal-fired factories or America 's auto traffic , all those carbon emissions were already producing signs of global warming that , by the 1990s , would set alarm bells ringing among scientists worldwide . From the " pre-industrial " @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 1880 , carbon dioxide concentrations in the atmosphere kept climbing to 410 ppm by 2018 , resulting in the rising seas , devastating fires , raging storms , and protracted droughts that came to be known as global warming . <p> As evidence of the climate crisis became undeniable , the world 's nations responded with striking unanimity by signing the 2015 Paris Climate Agreement to cut carbon emissions and surge investments into alternative energy that soon yielded significant breakthroughs in both cost and efficiency . Within four years , the International Energy Agency predicted that dramatic drops in the cost of solar panels meant that solar energy would soon be " the new king of the world 's electricity markets . " Indeed , as technology slashed the cost of battery storage and solar panels , the International Renewable Energy Agency reported in 2024 that the solar generation of electricity had become 41% cheaper than fossil fuels , while offshore wind was 53% cheaper -- a truly significant disparity that will , as technology continues to slash the cost of solar energy , render the use of coal and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ an utter absurdity . <p> In the game of empires , seemingly small margins can have large consequences , often marking the difference between dominance and subordination , success and failure -- whether the 35% advantage of enslaved over free labor , the 50% cost advantage for Dutch sailing craft over British ones , and now a 41% savings for solar over fossil fuels . Moreover , the day is fast coming when fossil-fuel electricity will cost more than twice as much as alternative energy from solar and wind power . <p> To assure America 's economic future , the administration of President Joe Biden began investing trillions of dollars in alternative energy by building battery plants , encouraging massive wind and solar projects , and continuing a consumer subsidy to sustain Detroit 's transition to electric vehicles . Given China 's recent progress in key energy sectors , the answer is a resounding yes . <p> Under its economic plan , China has already come to dominate the world 's solar power industry . In 2024 , it cut the wholesale price of its solar panel exports in half and nearly doubled its exports of panel components . To replace its old export " trio " of clothing , furniture , and appliances , Beijing has mandated a " new trio " of solar panels , lithium batteries , and electric cars . It portrays U Thant 's growing despair as the Security Council became captive to power politics , and budgetary starvation undermined the UN 's ability to act . His anguish during the Bangladesh crisis prefigured today 's helplessness over Gaza . <p> The answer to what is needed for the restoration of the UN 's relevance lies in what may be called the Trinity of Multilateral Responsibility , comprising three interdependent actors : The Secretariat , the Member States , and We @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ public goods on the basis of what PM Modi and India emphasise as the credo of " one Earth , one family , one future , " or Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam , the institution becomes the transcendental force it is meant to be . Secretaries-General such as U Thant exercised discretion and spoke truth to power without partiality . Today , political bias and bureaucratic control have replaced principled leadership in a polarised world . The Member States , especially the privileged P5 , were entrusted to support the UN as the custodian of GPGs ( global public goods ) and a champion of the disadvantaged . Instead , the most powerful countries have jettisoned GPGs , including sustainable development and aid to poor countries . Civil society , academia , the media , youth and women 's movements and the private sector once sustained this moral energy . Today , that civic engagement has withered into indifference . The End of Global Jewish Recruitment and the Slow Collapse of Zionist Identification Among the Young <p> For seventy-five years one of Israel 's quiet but decisive assets was the willingness of Jews around the world to identify with the state , defend it , fund it , and , when necessary , move to it and fight for it . That reservoir is drying up with a speed no government minister can publicly admit . <p> The numbers are stark . Aliyah from the West has fallen to its lowest level since the 1980s . " Mandatory IDF service , once the rite of passage into adulthood , is increasingly seen as " participation in occupation . The Collapse of U.S. Political Consensus <p> For decades , the single most durable external pillar of Israel 's strategic position was the illusion of an unshakable bipartisan consensus in Washington . That consensus has not merely eroded ; it has collapsed . <p> Among Democrats , the shift is explicit . Once-automatic support fractured under the weight of civilian devastation in Gaza , mass displacement , and violations of ceasefire terms . Senior members of Congress began publicly questioning weapons transfers ; younger lawmakers , shaped by movements from Ferguson to anti-Muslim-ban protests , redefined Palestinian rights as part of a broader struggle against racialized state violence . Even stalwarts like Chuck Schumer were forced to temper support , sensing the base had shifted . Tech leaders , donors , and university boards ? -- ? once predictable reservoirs of pro-Israel sentiment ? -- ? went quiet or pivoted to neutrality . <p> The think-tank world experienced upheaval . Analysts at Brookings and the Council on Foreign Relations published assessments questioning Israel 's strategic competence , long-term viability under permanent militarization , and the wisdom of binding U.S. credibility to a failing war . <p> Israel is no longer a consensus issue but an exposed one : a subject of partisan division , generational revolt , moral outrage , strategic doubt , and electoral risk . The bipartisan line of credit is gone , and with it the last external collateral that once allowed Israel to operate with an unlimited overdraft . What remains is an ally that can still extend arms shipments but can no longer underwrite the political risk . <p> VIII . The West Bank : A @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the graveyard of the old governing model ? -- ? the place where the thirty-year fiction of a " temporary , " " manageable , " and ultimately " reversible " occupation was buried once and for all . <p> What was sold to the world ( and to Israelis ) as an interim arrangement that could be traded away in a future peace deal has instead become a permanent , daily , unaffordable re-occupation with no political horizon , no willing Palestinian partner , and no international tolerance . The Deterrence Economy and Iran 's New Posture <p> For decades Israel sustained its regional dominance through what analysts once called the " deterrence economy " @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ military superiority , backed by the United States , would prevent adversaries like Iran and its allied networks from ever challenging Israel directly . But @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ That can send me spiralling . <p> But that disconnect , between the catastrophic and the trivial , is more common than I realised . It 's not apathy . It 's not a moral failure . It 's simply how our minds cope with living in a world that demands an impossible emotional bandwidth from us . <p> Psychologists call this feeling ' cognitive dissonance ' : the tension between knowing the world is burning and still worrying about everyday problems . <p> When everything is a crisis , nothing feels like one . <p> And there 's a coping mechanism called the ' spotlight effect ' , where your mind zooms in on the things that affect you directly , even if they are small . This is n't denial ; it 's survival . <h> Ambient catastrophe <p> We live in a time when the emotional toll of global bad news has quietly reshaped how we feel , think , and react . Every day brings a fresh wave of climate disasters , political turbulence , humanitarian crises , or violence -- all of it streaming directly @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ : a gradual numbing of our ability to care deeply about every single issue , because the alternative is emotional burnout . <p> It 's impossible to hold all the world 's suffering at once , so our brains triage . They narrow our focus to what feels manageable : the inbox , the deadline , the familiar stress of office life . Not because these things matter more , but because they 're the things we can control . <p> This also brings the familiar sense of guilt for not doing enough . For years , I blamed myself for what I thought was selective activism . I would rage about climate injustice but scroll past other horrors . I would read obsessively about Gaza , then take breaks when the grief overwhelmed me . I would worry about political regression and the normalisation of authoritarianism , yet in the same breath , would feel anxious about someone spoiling the season finale of Stranger Things . <p> But I now realise that this selective sensitivity , this ebb and flow of attention , is itself a human response to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of what some call " ambient catastrophe " , a time when crisis is always in the background -- never fully addressed , never fully gone . And it creates a strange emotional climate : part resignation , part numbness , part hyper-vigilance . <p> So all I can really think about is that one email . I ca n't seem to let go of it . <p> But I am also realising that focusing on an email over the distant , vague suffering of the world is also a form of unconscious self-compassion . <p> Tending to the small , immediate fires of our personal lives -- a mistake at work , a tense conversation with a friend , a day of self-doubt -- gives us structure . @@131952068 <h> Share : <p> In moments of historical crisis , political language becomes a battlefield . The words that are permitted , prohibited , or policed reveal the ideological architecture of power . Few debates illustrate this more starkly than the ongoing struggle over naming Zionism , Israeli state violence , the ongoing ethnic cleansing and genocide in Gaza and across Palestine , and the political usage of Jewish identity . For decades , dissident Jewish intellectuals -- Norman Finkelstein , Yeshayahu Leibowitz , and Hajo Meyer , amongst many others -- have pierced the ideological wall , insisting that one can not understand Israel without naming the moral catastrophes embedded within its very founding to the present times . <p> Their work remains indispensable today , as the Israeli state stands accused before the International Court of Justice , international jurists describe a " genocidal pattern , " and Western governments work overtime to criminalize criticism of Zionism through instruments like the IHRA definition of antisemitism . <p> This is not merely an academic debate -- it is a struggle over whether political truth can be spoken at all @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Need to Name <p> The Ideology of Jewish Exceptionalism <p> Central to the Zionist project has been the claim that the Jewish state stands outside ordinary political morality . Criticism is not simply disagreement -- it is framed as sacrilege . As a result , naming the violence of the Israeli state becomes , itself , a punishable act . <p> This is precisely why the three dissident thinkers at the heart of this article were so vilified : each insisted that no state -- including a Jewish one -- has the right to place itself outside moral scrutiny and international law . <p> Finkelstein : " The misuse of the Holocaust " <p> Norman Finkelstein 's landmark book " The Holocaust Industry " argued that political elites in Israel and the United States wield the memory of Jewish suffering as a shield to protect Israeli militarism. 1 As he famously wrote : <p> " The Holocaust has become an indispensable ideological weapon . Through its deployment , one of the world 's most formidable military powers has cast itself as a victim . " 2 <p> For this , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ power of the ideological taboo he exposed . <p> II . Yeshayahu Leibowitz and the " Judeo-Nazi " Warning <p> Perhaps no phrase provoked more outrage in Israeli society than when the Orthodox Israeli philosopher Yeshayahu Leibowitz warned , as early as 1968 , that the occupation of Palestinian land would produce a new political subject : <p> Leibowitz was not making a theological provocation . He was articulating a sociological law : military rule over a subjugated population leads inevitably to cruelty , racism , and a moral collapse indistinguishable from the very forces Jews suffered under in Europe . <p> Leibowitz , who had been nominated for the Israel Prize , was denounced as a traitor and fascist . His critics understood the danger of the analogy : once the " Judeo-Nazi " concept enters public discourse , the moral inviolability of the Israeli state collapses . And with it , the ideological foundations of Jewish supremacism . <p> III . " <h> What Is the Two-State Solution ? <p> The two-state solution is a highly publicised political process by which the Israeli-Palestinian conflict would be resolved by the establishment of two independent states-Israel and Palestine-within the borders of the former British Mandate of Palestine . <p> The plan involves Israel and an independent Palestine to co-exist in a given area with secure and internationally recognised borders . In most spoken scenarios , the land comprising an independent Palestine would include the West Bank and Gaza Strip and have East Jerusalem as its capital . <p> The notion of partitioning the territory into separate Jewish and Arab states originated in 1937 with the British Peel Commission , which for @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ tensions between the two communities . <p> A decade later , in 1947 , the United Nations adopted a partition plan that brought about the state of Israel and triggered the 1948 Arab-Israeli war . After the 1967 Six-Day War , Israel seized control of the West Bank , Gaza and East Jerusalem , areas that remain at the core of the conflict . <h> Why the Two-State Solution Remains Unresolved <p> From the 2000 Camp David Summit to the 2013-14 U.S.-led peace talks , the two-state solution has never been realized despite decades of diplomatic negotiations . There are several disputes over the demarcation of borders , the legal and political status of Jerusalem , the future of Israeli settlements in the West Bank , security arrangements , and the right of return for Palestinian refugees . <p> The Palestinian Authority still upholds a two-state solution based on 1967 borders , whereas the current Israeli government opposes Palestinian statehood . Netanyahu has said that the Palestinians may have limited autonomy but not full statehood . <p> Public support for the two-state concept fluctuates among both Israelis and Palestinians , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ political leadership and security concerns . <p> The October 2023 attack by Hamas on Israel and the ensuing Israeli offensive in Gaza have restarted debate around the world , with many analysts contending that without a political resolution , cycles of war and humanitarian crisis will continue . <h> Global Consequences and Appeal for Mediation by Pope Leo <p> With the regional dynamics continuing to shift , including growing discourses of normalization between Israel and Saudi Arabia , Palestinians fear the prospect of statehood slipping further away . Without a two-state framework , many international observers argue , the region risks long-term instability and a permanent one-state reality of conflict and occupation . <p> Pope Leo concluded his address by calling upon the international community 's leaders to commit to serious negotiations . He expressed hope that countries including the United States , Turkey , Russia and others could play critical roles in securing a ceasefire and a durable peace plan . " We try , with both sides , to help bring them closer to a solution with justice for all , " he said .
